Solo quelli iscritti nel Registro nazionale degli alimenti senza glutine del Ministero della Salute, nelle categorie previste: pane e prodotti da forno salati, pasta e pizza, preparati per dolci, pane e pizza, prodotti da forno dolci e cereali per la colazione. Il Prontuario AIC è un'altra cosa: è un elenco volontario di prodotti adatti ai celiaci, non l'elenco di quelli acquistabili con il buono.

La novità del 2026

L'articolo 77 della Legge di Bilancio 2026 rende il buono digitale e spendibile in tutta Italia, non più solo nella regione di residenza, man mano che le regioni attivano il nuovo sistema. I dettagli sono nel nostro articolo sulle novità normative 2026, mentre importi e detrazioni sono nella guida su quanto costa la dieta senza glutine.

Come organizzare la spesa

  • Usa il buono per i prodotti sostitutivi come pane, pasta, farine e prodotti da forno, che sono i più costosi.
  • Compra al supermercato gli alimenti naturalmente senza glutine, come riso, mais, legumi, verdure, carne e pesce.
  • Confronta i prezzi dello stesso prodotto tra farmacia, supermercato e negozio specializzato.
  • Controlla sempre la dicitura "senza glutine" in etichetta, qualunque sia il canale: vedi la guida su come leggere le etichette.
Per cercare un punto vendita o un locale nella tua zona vedi la guida a come trovare locali senza glutine vicino a te.

Se fai la spesa da solo in Italia, anche da turista

Bastano tre mosse. Riconosci i prodotti: cerca la dicitura «senza glutine» o la Spiga Barrata, e leggi l'elenco ingredienti (come leggere le etichette). Scegli il canale: i discount hanno linee dedicate, come «Amo Essere Senza Glutine» di Eurospin, «Enjoy Free» di Aldi e le referenze Realforno gluten free di Lidl, mentre farmacie e negozi specializzati hanno di solito l'assortimento più ampio (dettagli in spesa senza glutine al discount). Controlla ogni volta: l'assortimento cambia da negozio a negozio. Il buono mensile è una misura per i celiaci assistiti dal Servizio Sanitario Nazionale: se non lo sei, contano solo prezzo ed etichetta. Le regole in dettaglio sono nella pagina normativa sulla celiachia.

parts.title: Viaggi, famiglia e imprevisti
parts.intro: Quando si esce dalla routine: le vacanze, i bambini a scuola, lo svezzamento e cosa fare se il glutine arriva per errore.

chapters.title: Viaggiare senza glutine: 7 consigli per le vacanze sicure
takeaways: Cerca ristoranti e hotel certificati a destinazione prima di partire e salvali in una mappa condivisa.
Il tesserino AIC multilingue aiuta a comunicare la celiachia al personale di sala all'estero.
Richiedi i pasti gluten free in aereo con almeno 48 ore d'anticipo e porta sempre snack sicuri di scorta.
Le directory locali e le community online restano la risorsa più affidabile fuori dai circuiti turistici.
chapters.html:
Prima della partenza

Cercare in anticipo ristoranti e hotel certificati nella destinazione scelta, salvando gli indirizzi in una mappa condivisa, riduce lo stress durante il viaggio. Per un soggiorno in hotel o villaggio, la nostra guida su hotel e villaggi certificati AIC spiega cosa garantisce davvero la certificazione, mentre la rassegna delle migliori città italiane per una vacanza senza glutine aiuta a scegliere la meta.

Il tesserino di traduzione per celiaci

AIC mette a disposizione un tesserino con la spiegazione della celiachia tradotta in più lingue, utilissimo per comunicare con il personale di sala nei paesi esteri.

In aereo e in treno

Molte compagnie aeree offrono pasti gluten free su richiesta, da prenotare almeno 48 ore prima. Meglio comunque portare sempre snack sicuri per ogni evenienza. I dettagli sul pasto speciale GFML e su cosa portare a bordo sono nella guida su volare senza glutine.

Trovare locali sicuri sul posto

Le directory locali e le community online dedicate ai celiaci sono la risorsa più affidabile per scoprire attività verificate anche fuori dai circuiti turistici principali. Se viaggi verso l'Italia, c'è la guida Mangiare senza glutine in Italia: la guida per chi viene dall'estero.

Impara le parole chiave nella lingua del posto

Oltre al tesserino AIC, sapere come si dice "senza glutine" e "contaminazione" nella lingua locale aiuta a farsi capire anche in situazioni informali, come un bar o un mercato, dove il tesserino da solo può non bastare a chiarire la richiesta.

Scegli un alloggio con angolo cottura, se possibile

Un appartamento o una stanza con un piccolo angolo cottura permette di preparare in autonomia una parte dei pasti, riducendo la dipendenza dai ristoranti nei giorni più intensi del viaggio: utile soprattutto nelle mete meno turistiche, dove trovare locali verificati può richiedere più tempo.

Porta sempre una scorta extra di snack sicuri

Oltre agli snack per il volo, conviene avere una piccola scorta per tutta la durata del viaggio: ritardi, coincidenze o giornate imprevedibili possono lasciarti senza un pasto sicuro nelle vicinanze, soprattutto nelle prime ore in una città nuova.

chapters.title: Hotel e villaggi turistici certificati AIC per celiaci: come scegliere una vacanza senza pensieri
takeaways: Un hotel certificato AIC garantisce una colazione senza glutine sicura e staff formato sulla celiachia, non solo generiche "opzioni gluten free".
Nei villaggi con pensione completa la certificazione riguarda l'intera gestione dei pasti in cucina, non solo la colazione.
Anche senza certificazione, alcune strutture offrono cucine attrezzate in camera o accordi con ristoranti certificati nelle vicinanze.
Prenotare con anticipo e segnalare la celiachia al momento della prenotazione, non all'arrivo, resta la regola d'oro per una vacanza senza sorprese.
chapters.html:
Hotel certificati AIC: perché fanno la differenza in vacanza

In vacanza, la gestione della celiachia cambia rispetto alla routine di casa: non hai la tua cucina, mangi fuori più spesso e spesso in strutture che non conosci. Scegliere hotel e villaggi turistici certificati AIC per celiaci significa affidarsi a strutture che hanno superato controlli specifici su colazione, gestione della cucina e formazione del personale, invece di scoprire all'arrivo se la struttura è davvero attrezzata. In questa guida vediamo cosa garantisce realmente la certificazione e come organizzare una vacanza senza pensieri.

Cosa garantisce davvero un hotel certificato AIC

La certificazione non è un'etichetta generica: copre aspetti specifici e verificabili della struttura. Se vuoi capire nel dettaglio come funziona il programma AIC dietro questo marchio, anche per ristoranti e altri locali, vedi la nostra guida su cosa significa davvero "certificazione AIC".

Colazione senza glutine sicura

Pane, biscotti, cereali e dolci senza glutine preparati o conservati separatamente dagli altri prodotti, per evitare la contaminazione crociata tipica dei buffet condivisi.

Staff formato sulla celiachia

Il personale di sala e cucina riceve una formazione specifica su come gestire richieste e preparazioni senza glutine, riducendo il rischio di errori dovuti a disattenzione o scarsa conoscenza del tema.

Cucina attrezzata per pasti completi

Nelle strutture con ristorante interno, la certificazione può coprire anche pranzo e cena, con piatti preparati evitando il contatto con ingredienti contenenti glutine.

Villaggi turistici e pensione completa: cosa cambia rispetto a un hotel classico

Nei villaggi con pensione completa la gestione della celiachia è più complessa, perché coinvolge tutti i pasti della giornata, spesso in formula buffet.

Il rischio dei buffet condivisi

I buffet self-service, tipici dei villaggi turistici, aumentano il rischio di contaminazione: posate condivise tra vassoi diversi, briciole che passano da un piatto all'altro. Un villaggio certificato AIC prevede postazioni dedicate o personale che serve direttamente i piatti senza glutine.

Ristoranti a tema e show cooking

Le serate a tema e gli show cooking, molto diffusi nei villaggi, richiedono attenzione extra: verifica sempre con lo staff se sono previste alternative senza glutine per quella specifica serata, idealmente comunicandolo al check-in.

Come trovare hotel e villaggi certificati AIC per la tua vacanza

Il modo più affidabile è verificare la certificazione direttamente sul sito della struttura o chiedendo conferma prima di prenotare, evitando di fidarsi solo di autodichiarazioni generiche come "gluten free friendly" trovate su portali di prenotazione. L'elenco delle strutture aderenti al programma Alimentazione Fuori Casa di AIC è pubblicato nella guida cartacea, sul sito di AIC, dove è aggiornato in tempo reale, e nell'app gratuita per i soci, con la mappa dei locali. Nella directory di Mappa Senza Glutine trovi le strutture verificate, con indicazione chiara se la certificazione è confermata o meno.

Non solo hotel: B&B, agriturismi e case vacanze

Il programma di AIC non riguarda solo gli alberghi: tra le strutture aderenti ci sono affittacamere, agriturismi, B&B, case vacanze e villaggi turistici. Le strutture della rete sono monitorate periodicamente da professionisti che supportano il personale e verificano il mantenimento dei requisiti. Un esempio nella nostra directory è l'Hotel Al Piave a Venezia, nel sestiere di Castello, vicino a Piazza San Marco: è indicato come uno dei pochi alberghi della città con certificazione AIC e offre una colazione interamente senza glutine. Se stai pianificando una vacanza in città, vedi anche la guida Venezia senza glutine e le migliori città italiane per una vacanza senza glutine.

Cosa fare se l'hotel non è certificato AIC

Anche senza certificazione, una vacanza senza glutine è possibile con qualche accorgimento in più: verifica se la camera ha un angolo cottura o un piccolo frigo per conservare snack e prodotti sicuri portati da casa, cerca ristoranti certificati AIC o segnalati dalla community nella zona per pranzo e cena, e porta sempre con te una scorta di prodotti senza glutine per le emergenze, soprattutto in mete poco turistiche dove trovarli sul posto può essere difficile.

Domande frequenti su hotel e villaggi senza glutine

Le domande più comuni di chi organizza una vacanza da celiaco.

Cosa significa che un hotel è certificato AIC?

Significa che la struttura ha superato controlli specifici dell'Associazione Italiana Celiachia su colazione, eventuale ristorazione interna e formazione del personale, con verifiche periodiche nel tempo.

I villaggi con pensione completa sono sicuri per celiaci?

Possono esserlo se certificati AIC o con procedure dedicate per i buffet: senza queste garanzie, il rischio di contaminazione crociata nelle formule self-service è più alto rispetto a un ristorante à la carte.

Devo avvisare l'hotel della celiachia prima di arrivare?

Sì, è fortemente consigliato segnalarlo già in fase di prenotazione, non al check-in: la cucina ha bisogno di tempo per organizzare colazione e pasti in sicurezza, soprattutto nei periodi di alta stagione.

Cosa porto con me in vacanza se l'hotel non è certificato?

Una scorta di prodotti senza glutine di base (pane, snack, pasta) per le emergenze, soprattutto se la meta è poco turistica: può essere difficile trovarli sul posto fuori dalle grandi città.

chapters.title: Bambini celiaci a scuola: come gestire mensa e gite
takeaways: Il pasto senza glutine nelle mense scolastiche è un diritto garantito per legge, senza costi extra per la famiglia.
Basta il certificato medico in segreteria per concordare il menu con il servizio di ristorazione.
Informare gli insegnanti in anticipo e portare snack sicuri evita disagi durante le gite scolastiche.
Coinvolgere il bambino nella scelta di dolci gluten free aiuta a vivere la socialità senza sentirsi diverso.
chapters.html:
La mensa scolastica: cosa prevede la legge

In Italia il diritto al pasto senza glutine nelle mense scolastiche è garantito dalla legge 4 luglio 2005, n. 123, che impone a mense scolastiche, ospedaliere e di altre strutture pubbliche di somministrare, su richiesta, anche pasti senza glutine: è una normativa praticamente unica al mondo. In pratica basta presentare il certificato medico alla segreteria e concordare il menu con il servizio di ristorazione, senza costi aggiuntivi per la famiglia: la legge prevede infatti fondi nazionali distribuiti alle Regioni, destinati sia all'acquisto degli ingredienti senza glutine sia alla formazione del personale di cucina. Secondo l'ultima Relazione al Parlamento del Ministero della Salute, nel 2024 sono state 33.027 le mense pubbliche ad aver erogato pasti senza glutine, di cui 22.972 scolastiche. Per chi si sta avvicinando allo svezzamento, la guida su svezzamento e glutine spiega quando e come introdurlo secondo la ricerca più recente.

L'inclusione a tavola: perché non servono tavoli separati

Le linee guida dell'Associazione Italiana Celiachia sono chiare su un punto: il pasto senza glutine non va trattato come un'eccezione da isolare. Un bambino celiaco ha diritto a un pasto equilibrato e di qualità equivalente a quello dei compagni, consumato allo stesso tavolo, non a una tavolata separata: è un aspetto che riguarda tanto la sicurezza alimentare quanto il vissuto psicologico del bambino a scuola.

Gite e uscite didattiche

Informare per tempo gli insegnanti e, se necessario, fornire snack sicuri da portare con sé evita situazioni di disagio durante le uscite fuori dal contesto scolastico. Per idee pratiche sulla merenda di tutti i giorni, vedi la nostra guida su merenda scuola senza glutine.

Feste di compleanno e socialità

Coinvolgere il bambino nella scelta di dolci e snack gluten free da condividere con i compagni aiuta a vivere la socialità senza sentirsi diversi.

chapters.title: Svezzamento e glutine: quando introdurlo e cosa dice la ricerca
takeaways: Secondo le linee guida ESPGHAN il glutine può essere introdotto in qualsiasi momento tra i 4 e i 12 mesi di vita.
Gli studi hanno smentito l'idea che anticipare o ritardare il glutine riduca il rischio di sviluppare la celiachia.
Nemmeno la durata dell'allattamento al seno, né il fatto che prosegua durante lo svezzamento, incidono sull'insorgenza della malattia.
L'unico fattore di rischio certo resta quello genetico, legato alla regione HLA del DNA: per questo lo screening dei familiari di primo grado è raccomandato.
chapters.html:
Una raccomandazione che è cambiata nel tempo

Per anni ai genitori è stato detto che esisteva una "finestra ideale" per introdurre il glutine, e che rispettarla potesse proteggere il bambino dalla celiachia. È una delle indicazioni che la ricerca ha rivisto più profondamente: oggi sappiamo che il momento in cui il glutine entra nella dieta non modifica la probabilità di sviluppare la malattia. Capire cosa dicono davvero le linee guida aiuta a vivere lo svezzamento con meno ansia, soprattutto quando in famiglia c'è già un celiaco.

Cosa dicono le linee guida oggi

Il riferimento europeo è la Società Europea di Gastroenterologia, Epatologia e Nutrizione Pediatrica (ESPGHAN).

La finestra dei 4-12 mesi

Secondo ESPGHAN il glutine può essere introdotto in qualsiasi momento tra i 4 e i 12 mesi di vita, senza che una tempistica precisa all'interno di questa finestra risulti preferibile alle altre in termini di prevenzione.

Perché non serve rincorrere una data

Gli studi condotti su bambini a rischio genetico hanno mostrato che né l'introduzione precoce né quella tardiva cambiano la probabilità di sviluppare celiachia nell'infanzia. Un'introduzione tardiva sembra al più ritardare la comparsa dei sintomi, non prevenire la malattia.

E l'allattamento al seno?

Anche su questo la letteratura ha corretto una convinzione diffusa: la durata dell'allattamento e il fatto che prosegua o meno durante lo svezzamento non incidono sull'insorgenza della celiachia. Questo non toglie nulla al valore dell'allattamento per tutti gli altri motivi per cui è raccomandato: semplicemente, non va vissuto come uno strumento di prevenzione della celiachia, perché non lo è.

Cosa conta davvero: la genetica

L'unico fattore di rischio certo identificato finora è genetico, legato a una specifica regione del DNA nota come HLA. È il motivo per cui la celiachia ricorre nelle famiglie e per cui lo screening dei parenti di primo grado è raccomandato anche in assenza di sintomi. Se in famiglia ci sono già casi accertati, parlarne con il pediatra prima dello svezzamento è più utile che rincorrere il mese "giusto" per il primo biscotto. Quando poi arriva una diagnosi, la nostra guida su mensa e gite scolastiche copre la fase successiva.

Domande frequenti su svezzamento e glutine

I dubbi più comuni dei genitori, soprattutto quando c'è familiarità con la celiachia.

Devo ritardare il glutine se in famiglia c'è un celiaco?

Le evidenze attuali non supportano il ritardo come strategia protettiva: il glutine può essere introdotto nella finestra 4-12 mesi come per gli altri bambini. Quello che ha senso, in caso di familiarità, è parlarne con il pediatra e sapere quali sintomi monitorare.

Se mio figlio sviluppa la celiachia è colpa di come l'ho svezzato?

No. L'unico fattore di rischio certo è genetico: né il momento dell'introduzione del glutine né le modalità di allattamento determinano l'insorgenza della malattia.

Quanto glutine dare all'inizio?

Non esiste una quantità "protettiva" dimostrata: l'introduzione segue le normali indicazioni dello svezzamento, gradualmente e insieme agli altri alimenti, secondo le indicazioni del pediatra che segue il bambino.

chapters.title: Ingestione accidentale di glutine: cosa fare se un celiaco lo mangia per errore
takeaways: Non esiste un trattamento specifico che blocchi il glutine già ingerito: l'AIC consiglia di non farsi prendere dal panico.
I sintomi, quando ci sono, compaiono da una-due ore fino a 24-48 ore dopo; alcune persone non ne hanno affatto.
Bere acqua, riposare e tornare subito alla dieta senza glutine sono le indicazioni su cui le fonti concordano.
Se i sintomi non passano o gli episodi si ripetono, serve il medico. Questa guida è informativa e non sostituisce il parere medico.
chapters.html:
La risposta breve

Se un celiaco ingerisce glutine per errore, non esiste un trattamento specifico che lo blocchi. L'AIC consiglia di non farsi prendere dal panico e di aspettare che i sintomi passino: in genere, secondo l'AIC, si risolvono nel giro di qualche ora. Se i disturbi non passano da soli, è il medico a valutare le terapie per i sintomi. Questa guida è informativa e non sostituisce il parere del medico.

Quali sintomi possono comparire e quando

I sintomi più descritti sono dolori addominali, mal di testa, diarrea, nausea o vomito, malessere generale e stanchezza. Possono comparire da una o due ore dopo l'assunzione fino a 24 ore, e in molti casi anche a distanza di 24-48 ore. Quanto durano varia: le fonti non sono allineate, e vanno da poche ore a diversi giorni. Non tutti hanno sintomi: alcune persone non ne avvertono nessuno, ma il danno all'intestino può comunque verificarsi, ed è per questo che l'assenza di sintomi non è un via libera.

Cosa puoi fare nelle ore successive

Le fonti concordano su poche cose semplici:

  • Bere acqua, soprattutto in presenza di vomito o diarrea.
  • Riposare e mangiare leggero finché il malessere passa.
  • Tornare subito alla dieta senza glutine, senza altre eccezioni.
Per i farmaci non diamo indicazioni: i disturbi si trattano solo su consiglio del medico.

Quando sentire il medico

Conviene contattare il medico o il gastroenterologo che ti segue se i sintomi non passano, se sono molto forti o se gli episodi si ripetono. Vale la pena anche segnalargli le esposizioni accidentali, soprattutto se ti accorgi che succedono spesso: possono indicare un punto della tua routine da correggere. Per capire meglio la malattia c'è la guida a cos'è la celiachia.

Come evitare che succeda

Quasi sempre l'errore nasce da una contaminazione o da un'etichetta letta male. A casa conta la contaminazione crociata in cucina, fuori casa come evitarla al ristorante, e per i prodotti confezionati come leggere le etichette e la guida agli ingredienti dubbi. I locali che aderiscono al programma AIC seguono procedure condivise con l'associazione: li trovi sulla mappa dei ristoranti AIC.

parts.title: Understanding celiac disease
parts.intro: Before changing what's on your table it helps to understand what happens in the body: what celiac disease is, how it differs from other conditions and where gluten hides.

chapters.title: Celiac Disease: What It Is, Symptoms and How It's Diagnosed
takeaways: Celiac disease is an autoimmune condition triggered by gluten, not a food allergy or intolerance.
Diagnosis requires blood tests and a duodenal biopsy: don't remove gluten from your diet before completing them.
The only treatment is a lifelong gluten-free diet, which allows symptoms to go into remission.
Screening is recommended for first-degree relatives too, given the genetic component of the disease.
chapters.html:
What is celiac disease

Celiac disease is an autoimmune condition triggered by ingesting gluten, the protein found in wheat, barley and rye. In genetically predisposed people, gluten triggers an immune response that damages the intestinal villi, impairing nutrient absorption.

How common it is in Italy

According to the Italian Ministry of Health's report to Parliament, in 2024 diagnosed celiacs in Italy reached almost 280,000 (85,238 men and 194,274 women), a national prevalence of 0.47% of the population, with over 14,000 new diagnoses that year. AIC estimates the real number of celiacs is much higher, around 600,000 in total: more than half still without a diagnosis.

The genetic component: the HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8 genes

Predisposition to celiac disease is linked to the HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8 genes: almost all celiacs carry them, although carrying them doesn't automatically mean developing the disease. This genetic component is exactly why screening is recommended for first-degree relatives, as noted later in this guide.

The most common symptoms

Symptoms vary widely from person to person and can appear at any age. If you're wondering whether you have a problem with gluten, also read our guide to gluten intolerance.

Gastrointestinal symptoms

Bloating, abdominal pain, alternating diarrhea and constipation, and nausea are the most frequent signs, especially in children.

Extraintestinal symptoms

Chronic fatigue, iron-deficiency anemia, dermatitis herpetiformis, recurring mouth ulcers and early osteoporosis are typical in adults.

How diagnosis works

Diagnosis is based on blood tests for anti-transglutaminase antibodies, followed by an endoscopy with duodenal biopsy to confirm damage to the intestinal villi. It's essential not to remove gluten from the diet before completing all tests. In men, diagnosis tends to arrive later than in women on average: we cover this in our guide on celiac disease in men. It's also worth not confusing celiac disease with non-celiac gluten sensitivity: the differences are explained in our guide on gluten sensitivity vs. celiac disease.

After diagnosis: the gluten-free diet

The only effective treatment available today is a strictly gluten-free diet for life. Over time the intestinal lining regenerates and symptoms subside. Relying on AIC-certified venues and products helps avoid cross-contamination in everyday life. Some life stages call for specific attention: we cover this, for example, in our guide on celiac disease and pregnancy. If you eat gluten by mistake, our guide to what to do after accidental ingestion explains what to expect.

chapters.title: Gluten Sensitivity or Celiac Disease? The Differences You Need to Know
takeaways: Celiac disease is an autoimmune condition with documentable intestinal damage; gluten sensitivity is not.
Non-celiac gluten sensitivity causes similar symptoms but without the antibodies or villous damage typical of celiac disease.
Wheat allergy is a third, distinct condition, immune-mediated but not autoimmune, with reactions that can occur quickly after ingestion.
Only a medical diagnosis, not self-assessment of symptoms, can reliably distinguish between the three conditions.
chapters.html:
Why it's easy to confuse celiac disease and gluten sensitivity

Bloating, fatigue, headaches and intestinal discomfort after eating gluten-containing foods can have very different origins, and it's common for people experiencing them to wonder whether it's celiac disease, simple sensitivity, or something else. Correctly distinguishing between these conditions isn't just a matter of terminology: it radically changes the diagnostic path and day-to-day management. In everyday language, all three are often called gluten intolerance.

Celiac disease: an autoimmune condition with documentable damage

Celiac disease is an autoimmune condition in which gluten triggers an immune response that damages the intestinal villi, damage that can be detected with specific blood tests and confirmed with a duodenal biopsy. It's the only one of the three conditions with an objective, internationally standardized diagnostic path.

Non-celiac gluten sensitivity: similar symptoms, different mechanism

A real but still less understood condition than celiac disease, which deserves to be carefully distinguished.

How it shows up

People with non-celiac gluten sensitivity can have symptoms very similar to celiac disease, such as bloating, abdominal pain and fatigue, but without the specific antibodies of celiac disease or the villous damage found on biopsy.

How it's diagnosed

There's no specific test for gluten sensitivity: diagnosis is reached by exclusion, after ruling out celiac disease and wheat allergy with the appropriate tests, then observing symptom improvement on a gluten-free diet.

Wheat allergy: a third condition, not to be confused with the first two

Wheat allergy is an immune reaction mediated by IgE antibodies, similar to other food allergies, which can appear quickly after ingestion with symptoms like hives, swelling or, in more severe cases, breathing difficulties. Unlike celiac disease, it doesn't concern gluten alone but wheat proteins as a whole, and is diagnosed with specific allergy tests such as skin prick tests or specific IgE blood tests.

Why a medical diagnosis is always essential

Removing gluten from your diet without a clear diagnosis carries more than one concrete risk:

  • It makes a celiac disease diagnosis impossible, since testing requires gluten to still be present in the diet.
  • It can mask other conditions that require specific treatment beyond diet alone.
  • It risks leading to an unbalanced diet if started without the support of a specialist or nutritionist.
That's why, faced with persistent symptoms after eating gluten, the first step should always be a medical evaluation, not removing gluten from your diet on your own.

chapters.title: Gluten: What It Is, Where It's Found and Why Some People Must Avoid It
takeaways: Gluten is a protein complex made of gliadins and glutenins, which form the elastic network typical of doughs when mixed with water.
It's found in wheat (soft and durum), barley, rye, farro, spelt, Khorasan wheat (often sold as KAMUT®) and triticale.
Rice, corn, buckwheat, millet, quinoa, amaranth, sorghum and teff are naturally gluten-free; oats are a special case.
For people without celiac disease, wheat allergy or gluten sensitivity, there's no evidence that cutting out gluten brings benefits.
chapters.html:
What gluten is

Gluten is a complex of proteins found in some grains. It forms when two groups of wheat proteins, gliadins and glutenins, come into contact with water and are worked: together they create an elastic network that traps the gases produced during rising. That's why bread dough stretches without tearing and pasta holds its shape when cooked. For people with celiac disease, the part that triggers the reaction is the fraction called prolamin, which has a different name in each grain: gliadin in wheat, secalin in rye, hordein in barley, avenin in oats.

Grains that contain gluten

According to the Italian Celiac Association (AIC), the grains to avoid are:

  • Wheat, both soft and durum, and all its derivatives (plain flour, semolina, breadcrumbs, couscous, bulgur)
  • Barley, including barley malt
  • Rye
  • Farro and spelt
  • Khorasan wheat, often sold under the KAMUT® brand
  • Triticale, a cross between wheat and rye
Farro and Kamut are sometimes marketed as "lighter" alternatives to wheat: for someone with celiac disease they aren't, because they contain gluten just like wheat. For the full list of allowed and forbidden foods, see our guide to what a celiac can eat.

Naturally gluten-free grains

Many grains and pseudocereals contain no gluten in nature: rice, corn, buckwheat (which, despite its name, isn't wheat), millet, quinoa, amaranth, sorghum and teff. Potatoes, legumes and chestnuts are also naturally gluten-free. The risk of contamination during processing remains, though: rice flour milled in a plant that also handles wheat isn't safe unless it's labeled "gluten-free". To see how to use them in the kitchen, read our guide to gluten-free flours. Oats deserve a separate discussion, which you'll find in our article do oats contain gluten? For the doubtful cases, like farro, couscous and rice, see our guide to Is it gluten-free? Rice, farro, couscous and Nutella.

Where gluten hides

Avoiding regular bread and pasta is the easy part: gluten also shows up where you wouldn't expect it. To debunk the most common myths, see our true-or-false guide to gluten. Inhaled gluten, instead, is not a risk for people with celiac disease according to AIC: see can someone with celiac disease be a baker or pizza maker?.

In processed foods

It can be used as a thickener, binder or flavoring in ready-made sauces, stock cubes, cured meats, ready meals, ice cream, sweets and barley- or malt-based drinks, as well as, of course, regular beer.

Through cross-contamination

Even a naturally gluten-free food becomes risky if it's cooked with utensils, cutting boards, frying oil or cooking water shared with foods that contain gluten. Practical rules for avoiding this are in our guide to cross-contamination in the kitchen.

How to spot it on the label

EU Regulation 1169/2011 requires gluten-containing grains, which are among the 14 main allergens, to be highlighted in the ingredient list. The "gluten-free" claim, on the other hand, can only be used under EU Regulation 828/2014 if the product contains no more than 20 mg/kg of gluten. All the details are in our guide on how to read food labels.

Is gluten bad for you? Only for some people

Gluten isn't harmful to everyone: it causes problems for people with one of these three different conditions.

  • Celiac disease: an autoimmune disease in which gluten damages the villi of the small intestine. We cover it in our guide on what celiac disease is.
  • Wheat allergy: an allergic reaction mediated by IgE antibodies, involving wheat proteins in general.
  • Non-celiac gluten sensitivity: symptoms similar to celiac disease without intestinal damage, diagnosed by exclusion.
In everyday language, these conditions are often all called gluten intolerance. For people who don't have any of them, there's no evidence that cutting out gluten is beneficial: we also cover this in our article does a gluten-free diet help you lose weight?

Get tested before cutting it out

If you suspect gluten makes you unwell, don't remove it from your diet on your own. Celiac tests only work if you're still eating gluten: cutting it out beforehand can make antibody levels drop and produce a false negative, making diagnosis much harder. The first step is to talk to your GP.

parts.title: What to eat and how to read labels
parts.intro: Everyday choices go through the label. This part lines up the safe foods, the ones to avoid and the cases that confuse people most.

chapters.title: What Can a Celiac Eat? The Complete Guide to Safe and Unsafe Foods
takeaways: Grains like wheat, barley, rye and their derivatives should always be avoided: they're the main sources of gluten in the Italian diet.
Rice, corn, buckwheat, quinoa and legumes are naturally gluten-free and can be eaten freely.
Many processed foods (sauces, stock cubes, cold cuts) can contain hidden gluten: always check the label or the AIC Food Guide.
The Crossed Grain symbol on packaging remains the fastest way to spot a safe product on the shelf.
chapters.html:
What does "eating gluten-free" really mean

Getting a celiac disease diagnosis means rethinking your grocery shopping and kitchen habits from scratch, and in the first weeks the most common question is always the same: what can I actually eat without risk? The good news is that there are plenty of naturally gluten-free foods, and the diet can stay varied and enjoyable. The real challenge lies in processed foods, where gluten can hide in ingredients you wouldn't expect, like thickeners, stock cubes or ready-made sauces. For a fuller picture on macronutrients, see our guide on a balanced gluten-free diet.

Foods that are always safe for a celiac

These are the food groups you can rely on without worry, naturally gluten-free.

Gluten-free grains and flours

Rice, corn, buckwheat, quinoa, amaranth, millet and the flours made from them are naturally gluten-free and form the safe backbone of a celiac's diet, as long as they haven't been contaminated during processing or packaging. To learn how to use them best in the kitchen, our guide to gluten-free flours compares the main alternatives to plain wheat flour.

Fresh fruit, vegetables, meat and fish

Fresh fruit and vegetables, meat, fish and plain eggs contain no gluten: the risk only appears if they're breaded, floured, or cooked alongside gluten-containing foods on the same surface.

Legumes and nuts

Legumes such as chickpeas, lentils and beans, as well as plain nuts, are safe and provide an excellent source of plant protein and fiber in a gluten-free diet.

Foods to always avoid

On the other hand, these foods naturally contain gluten and should always be excluded from a celiac's diet.

Wheat, barley, rye and their derivatives

Wheat, spelt, barley, rye, kamut and their derivatives (bread, pasta, pizza, traditional biscuits) contain gluten and should always be avoided, unless explicitly formulated and certified gluten-free.

Oats: a special case

Oats don't naturally contain gluten, but are often contaminated during growing or processing: only eat oats specifically certified "gluten-free" on the packaging. All the details are in our article do oats contain gluten?

Hidden-risk foods: when you need to read the label

Some processed products can contain gluten even when you'd least expect it:

  • Ready-made sauces and condiments, often thickened with wheat flour.
  • Stock cubes and soup mixes, which may contain wheat starch.
  • Cold cuts and cured meats, where gluten can appear as a thickener or flavoring.
  • Ice cream and industrial desserts, due to wafers, crumbled biscuits or wheat-based thickeners.
  • Traditional beer, made with malted barley, unlike certified gluten-free beers.
In all these cases, there's only one golden rule: always check the label or consult the AIC Food Guide before buying. You'll find all the details on how to do that in our guide on how to read food labels.

How to recognize a safe product: the Crossed Grain symbol and label wording

The Crossed Grain symbol, managed by AIC, is the fastest way to spot a product verified annually on the shelf. Alternatively, the "gluten-free" claim is regulated at the European level and guarantees a content below 20 ppm, the safety threshold recognized even for the most sensitive celiacs. To discover the most interesting new arrivals on the shelves, see our roundup gluten-free products: 2026's new arrivals.

chapters.title: How to Read Food Labels If You Have Celiac Disease
takeaways: The Crossed Grain symbol is the fastest way to spot an AIC-verified product on the shelf.
Starch, flavorings and yeast can hide gluten: check the AIC Food Guide whenever you're unsure.
The 'gluten-free' claim is regulated in Europe and guarantees a content below 20 ppm.
Even a certified product can get contaminated at home: use dedicated utensils for gluten-free prep.
chapters.html:
The Crossed Grain symbol

The Crossed Grain is the trademark registered by the Italian Celiac Association (AIC) that identifies products subject to strict annual auditing. It's the fastest and most reliable way to recognize a safe product on the shelf.

Ingredients to watch out for

Some ingredients require attention because they can hide gluten even in unsuspected products. For the most confusing cases, like wheat starch, soy sauce and yeast, see our guide Does it contain gluten? The doubtful ingredients.

Starch and modified starch

If the source isn't specified (corn, rice), starch may come from wheat: in Europe regulations still require gluten to be declared as an allergen, but checking remains important.

Flavorings and yeast

Yeast and barley malt extract can contain gluten: always check for the 'gluten-free' wording or the AIC Food Guide if in doubt.

Soy sauce and ready-made condiments

Traditional soy sauce is fermented with wheat and is one of the most overlooked sources of gluten, along with stock cubes and ready-made sauces thickened with flour.

"Gluten-free" and "very low gluten content": two different claims

Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 828/2014 governs both claims, and it's important not to confuse them. The "gluten-free" claim is only allowed if the content doesn't exceed 20 mg/kg (20 ppm) in the product as sold to the final consumer. There's also the "very low gluten content" claim, reserved for foods made from gluten-containing ingredients specially processed to reduce gluten, with a higher threshold of up to 100 mg/kg: a product labeled this way doesn't offer the same level of safety as "gluten-free" and should be assessed more carefully.

The AIC Food Guide: how to use it

The Food Guide is the app and yearly volume that lists thousands of products verified by AIC, updated monthly. It's the most complete tool for shopping safely, even for brands that don't carry the logo on the label. For a complete picture of what's safe to eat and what isn't, see our guide on what a celiac can eat.

Watch out for cross-contamination in the kitchen

Even a certified product can be contaminated if handled with non-dedicated utensils. In the kitchen it helps to have a cutting board, toaster and set of pots reserved exclusively for gluten-free preparation.

chapters.title: Does It Contain Gluten? Wheat Starch, Soy Sauce, Yeast and Other Doubtful Ingredients
takeaways: Ordinary wheat starch is not suitable for someone with celiac disease; deglutinated starch, under 20 ppm, is suitable according to AIC, but only in products declared gluten-free.
Traditional soy sauce contains wheat; «gluten-free» tamari is the safe choice.
Baker's yeast, dry or fresh, is not at risk; sourdough depends on the flour it's made with.
DOP and IGP balsamic vinegar is considered safe by AIC; gelatin and agar need checking on the product.
chapters.html:
Why ingredients can be misleading

On a label, gluten isn't always called «gluten»: it hides behind names like starch, yeast or sauce. On packaged food, cereals containing gluten must be highlighted in the ingredient list, but the ingredient itself isn't always easy to judge. In this guide we line up the cases that confuse people most, reporting what the Italian Celiac Association (AIC) says. For actual grains, like rice, farro and couscous, there is our guide Is it gluten-free? Rice, farro, couscous and Nutella; for the general method, the one on reading food labels.

Wheat starch: does it contain gluten?

Ordinary wheat starch keeps traces of gluten after extraction, and isn't suitable for someone with celiac disease. There is however deglutinated wheat starch, treated to fall below 20 ppm (20 mg of gluten per kilo): according to AIC it is suitable, provided the product containing it is declared gluten-free. A minority of people with celiac disease avoid it as a precaution. Rule of thumb: if the label says «wheat starch» and the product isn't declared «gluten-free» or doesn't carry the Crossed Grain mark, someone with celiac disease doesn't buy it.

Soy sauce and tamari

Traditional soy sauce is made with soy and wheat, so it contains gluten. The alternative is tamari, made without wheat and sold with the «gluten-free» wording: the label still needs checking, because not all tamari is the same and some may have traces of wheat. If you eat sushi or Asian food, our guide to gluten-free sushi, Chinese and Indian food explains how to handle it at a restaurant.

Brewer's yeast, sourdough and raising agents

According to AIC, baker's yeast (called «lievito di birra» in Italian), dry, freeze-dried or fresh, carries no gluten risk, despite the name: today it is a single-celled fungus (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) and no longer comes from beer. The exception is fresh liquid yeast, which is not pure yeast but a preparation with several ingredients and should be considered at risk unless labelled «gluten-free». Sourdough depends on the flour: if it's made with wheat flour it contains gluten, if it's made only with gluten-free flours it can be gluten-free. In ordinary commercial products «sourdough» is not a guarantee of no gluten.

Balsamic vinegar

For AIC you can safely eat Traditional Balsamic Vinegar DOP from Modena and Reggio Emilia, Balsamic Vinegar of Modena IGP, and non-DOP, non-IGP balsamic condiments made only of cooked grape must, wine vinegar and sulphites. For flavoured vinegars or those with other additives, suitability has to be checked product by product.

Gelatin, agar and pectin: it depends on the product

For these thickeners we don't give a flat answer, because it depends on processing. The FAQ of a regional AIC branch says gelatin should be used only if it appears in the AIC food handbook (Prontuario), and distinguishes leaf agar (usable) from bar agar (at risk). Pectin in itself contains no gluten, but it is used as an ingredient in products that may not be gluten-free: what counts is the finished product. The reference remains the AIC Prontuario and the label.

What to do when in doubt

  • Read the label and look for «gluten-free» or the Crossed Grain mark.
  • Check the AIC Prontuario for products that don't declare it.
  • Write to the manufacturer if that's not enough: it's free and they usually answer.
  • When in doubt, don't buy it: a cautious choice costs less than contamination. If it has already happened, see our guide to what to do after accidentally eating gluten.

chapters.title: Is It Gluten-Free? Rice, Farro, Couscous, Nutella and Other Tricky Foods
takeaways: Rice is naturally gluten-free; farro and traditional couscous are not, because they come from wheat.
A food can only be called «gluten-free» if it contains less than 20 mg per kilo.
For a branded product like Nutella there is no yes that holds forever: recipes and plants change, so what counts is the label on the jar in your hand.
When in doubt the label beats memory: look for gluten cereals highlighted in the ingredient list, the «gluten-free» wording or the Crossed Grain mark.
chapters.html:
The basic rule: what contains gluten and what doesn't

Gluten is found in wheat, barley and rye and in their derivatives; the full list is in our guide Gluten: what it is and where it's found. Everything that doesn't come from these cereals, meaning rice, corn, legumes, potatoes, vegetables, fruit, fresh meat and fish, and eggs, is naturally gluten-free. The doubts arise in the in-between cases: cereals with unclear names, processed foods and branded products.

Is rice gluten-free?

Yes: rice, in all its varieties, is naturally free of gluten, which is why it is the base of so many products for people with celiac disease, such as pasta, flour and bread. The gluten that is sometimes found «in rice» doesn't come from the rice: it comes from processing or from the kitchen. A risotto made with stock cubes, for example, needs checking because some stock cubes contain gluten cereals, and rice cooked in pots or water used for regular pasta gets contaminated. For packaged rice, just read the label: if it says «may contain traces of gluten», someone with celiac disease avoids it.

Is farro gluten-free?

No. In Italy «farro» covers several ancient wheat species, such as emmer, spelt and einkorn: they are all wheat, they contain gluten and they are off-limits for people with celiac disease. This applies to farro flour, pasta, bread and flakes. It is often perceived as lighter or easier to tolerate than common wheat, but for someone with celiac disease it makes no difference.

Is couscous gluten-free?

The traditional kind is not: it is made from durum wheat semolina, so it contains gluten. Gluten-free couscous does exist, made from corn or rice, and is recognised by the label («gluten-free» wording or the Crossed Grain mark). Be careful with ready meals and ethnic restaurants: the couscous served by default is the wheat one. The same goes for related grains: bulgur and seitan come from wheat, and barley contains gluten.

Polenta, quinoa, buckwheat: naturally gluten-free, but be careful

Corn (and therefore polenta), quinoa, amaranth, millet and buckwheat are naturally free of gluten: despite the name, buckwheat is not a wheat. The risk is contamination, because these grains are often processed in the same plants as wheat: for someone with celiac disease, the version bearing the «gluten-free» wording is the one that counts. For alternative flours there is our guide to gluten-free flours, while oats, a case of their own, have a dedicated guide.

Is Nutella gluten-free? Why we won't give you a flat yes

For branded products the answer depends on a recipe and a plant that the company can change, and information online isn't always aligned. On Nutella the sources we consulted disagree: some describe it as suitable for people with celiac disease because it has no gluten ingredients, others point out that the jar doesn't carry a «gluten-free» wording and that traces may be present. That's why we don't give you a yes or no that holds forever. What to do: read the label on the jar in your hand, look for «gluten-free» or the Crossed Grain mark, and check AIC's up-to-date guidance (AIC is the Italian Celiac Association). The same method applies to any other spread, snack or branded ice cream.

How to check a label in 30 seconds

  • Ingredient list: cereals containing gluten (wheat, barley, rye, farro, kamut) must be highlighted, for example in bold.
  • «Gluten-free» wording: it can appear only if the product contains less than 20 mg per kilo.
  • «May contain traces of gluten»: someone with celiac disease avoids it as a precaution.
  • Crossed Grain mark: AIC's mark guaranteeing that limit is respected.
The full method is in our guide to reading food labels. For wheat starch, soy sauce and yeast see Does it contain gluten? The doubtful ingredients.

chapters.title: Do Oats Contain Gluten? What People with Celiac Disease Can Really Eat
takeaways: Oats don't contain the same proteins as wheat: their prolamin, avenin, is tolerated by most people with celiac disease.
The real risk is contamination with wheat, barley or rye during growing, transport and milling.
Under EU Regulation 828/2014, oats can only be used in a "gluten-free" product if produced to avoid contamination and with no more than 20 mg/kg of gluten.
AIC advises eating only oats labeled "gluten-free" and introducing them under medical supervision, because a small share of celiacs can react to avenin.
chapters.html:
The short answer

Oats themselves don't contain gluten in the strict sense: their main protein is avenin, which is different from wheat gliadin, and most people with celiac disease tolerate it without problems. The problem is almost always something else: regular oats are grown, transported and milled alongside wheat, barley and rye, and end up contaminated. That's why regular supermarket oats aren't safe for people with celiac disease, while oats produced in a dedicated supply chain and labeled "gluten-free" are, for most people. For the broader picture on grains, see what gluten is and where it's found.

What EU rules say

EU Implementing Regulation 828/2014, which governs gluten-free claims on food, has a specific rule for oats: when they're used in a product labeled "gluten-free" or "very low gluten", they must have been specially produced, prepared or processed to avoid contamination by wheat, rye, barley or their crossbred varieties, and their gluten content must not exceed 20 mg/kg. To learn how to read these claims, see our guide to food labels for people with celiac disease.

AIC's position

The Italian Celiac Association explains that most people with celiac disease can eat oats without negative effects, but a small percentage may react to avenin. For this reason AIC recommends two things: choose only oat products labeled "gluten-free", and start eating them under medical supervision, so a doctor can assess any individual sensitivity and advise against them if needed. It remains a topic on which scientific research is still ongoing.

Regular oats vs gluten-free oats: how to tell them apart

On the shelf the two look very similar, but for people with celiac disease the difference is significant.

Regular oat flakes and flour

If the pack doesn't say "gluten-free", the oats should be considered contaminated and avoided. The label often also carries warnings such as "may contain traces of gluten".

Certified gluten-free oats

They carry the "gluten-free" claim under EU Regulation 828/2014 on the label and often the Crossed Grain (Spiga Barrata) mark. These are the only oats to use on a gluten-free diet.

Oat drinks, cookies and granola

The same rule applies: an oat drink, cookie or granola isn't automatically gluten-free just because it's made with oats. Only the claim on the label counts.

How to use gluten-free oats in the kitchen

Once your doctor has confirmed you can eat them, gluten-free oats are a versatile ingredient: flakes for porridge or yogurt at breakfast, flour to partly replace the mix in gluten-free cookies, or homemade granola. Keep utensils and containers separate from gluten-containing products, so you don't undo the benefit of buying them certified.

parts.title: In the kitchen and eating out
parts.intro: It doesn't take much gluten to do damage: a few crumbs are enough. Here you learn to manage the home kitchen, a dinner with friends and the restaurant.

chapters.title: Cross-Contamination in the Kitchen: Golden Rules for a Safe Home
takeaways: Even a few milligrams of gluten can trigger a reaction in celiacs: crumbs or shared utensils are enough.
Cutting boards, toasters and colanders should always be dedicated, or washed thoroughly before use.
In the pantry, keep gluten-free products in closed, clearly labeled containers, separate from the rest.
Wash hands, work surfaces and utensils between preparing gluten and gluten-free dishes.
chapters.html:
Why cross-contamination is dangerous

For a celiac, even trace amounts of gluten equal to a few crumbs can trigger an immune response and damage the intestinal villi: that's why cross-contamination needs the same attention as removing gluten directly from the diet.

The riskiest utensils

Some kitchen tools easily trap flour or crumb residue and need particular care.

Toasters and grills

The toaster is one of the riskiest items: it's best to have one dedicated exclusively to gluten-free bread, or use dedicated toaster bags.

Cutting boards and colanders

Wooden cutting boards and pasta colanders easily trap gluten residue in their pores: it's best to have dedicated versions, perhaps a different color so they're easy to spot at a glance.

Organizing the pantry

Storing gluten-free products in closed, clearly labeled containers, ideally on a separate shelf, reduces the risk of accidental contact with traditional flour or bread, especially in a kitchen shared with non-celiac family members.

Good daily habits

Always washing hands, work surfaces and utensils thoroughly between preparing a dish with gluten and one without, and cooking gluten-free food first when sharing the same stove, are simple habits that dramatically reduce the risk. If you have a celiac guest for dinner, see our etiquette guide to hosting a celiac friend.

Cooking water and frying oil: two often-overlooked risks

Cooking gluten-free pasta in water already used for traditional pasta contaminates it, even if the water looks clean: always use fresh water. The same goes for frying oil: a fryer or pan used for foods breaded with wheat flour contaminates anything fried in it afterward, potatoes included, even if the starting ingredient is naturally gluten-free.

Sponges and dish towels: an easy one to forget

Dish sponges and kitchen towels easily trap flour residue and need careful handling: it's best to have a sponge dedicated to gluten-free dishware, or at least wash it thoroughly before reusing it, and avoid drying dedicated cutting boards or utensils with a towel also used for traditional bread.

chapters.title: Hosting a Celiac Friend for Dinner: How to Get It Right Without the Awkwardness
takeaways: Asking is the right move: no celiac friend is offended if you ask what they can eat.
The simplest menu is built from naturally gluten-free foods, avoiding sauces and ready-made products you haven't checked.
The risk is in the details: cooking water, colander, chopping board, toaster, frying oil.
At a restaurant one clear sentence and three questions are enough: you can say it calmly, without seeming difficult.
chapters.html:
First of all: ask, don't guess

The first polite gesture is to ask. Ask your friend what they usually eat, whether there are brands or products they trust and whether they'd rather bring something from home. It isn't an insult: for someone with celiac disease, trusting an amateur cook is an act of trust, and a direct question shows you take it seriously. Better still, after dinner they'll tell you honestly how it went.

A simple menu, with naturally gluten-free ingredients

The safest way not to get it wrong is to cook with foods that contain no gluten by nature: fresh meat and fish, rice, potatoes, vegetables, legumes, eggs and fruit. Avoid ready-made sauces, stock cubes, breading and processed products whose label you haven't read: gluten hides in ingredients you don't expect, as we explain in Does it contain gluten? The doubtful ingredients. If you want to buy pasta or bread, pick products labelled «gluten-free» or bearing the Crossed Grain mark (reading food labels).

The kitchen: the risks you can't see

Gluten doesn't take much to do damage: a few crumbs are enough. Before cooking for a celiac guest:

  • Use new or well-washed water and pots for the gluten-free dish: the water you cooked regular pasta in won't do.
  • Colanders, chopping boards and wooden spoons are the trickiest, because porous material holds residue.
  • A shared toaster and butter: crumbs pass from one slice to another.
  • Frying oil shouldn't be reused if you've fried breaded food in it.
  • Sponges and cloths can carry gluten onto the worktop.
Cook the gluten-free dish first, with clean utensils, and keep it covered. More precautions in our guide to cross-contamination in the kitchen.

At the table: how to behave

Bring the gluten-free dish to the table first and don't let it touch the others: no shared spoon and no bread basket nearby. Don't serve bread or fries next to their plate. Above all, never say «a little piece won't hurt»: for someone with celiac disease it isn't true, and even people who feel nothing can have intestinal damage. If it happens by mistake, our guide to what to do after accidental ingestion explains what to expect.

At a restaurant: what to say without seeming difficult

If you're the one booking for a group with a celiac friend, choose a venue from the AIC restaurants map and call ahead. On the phone one calm sentence is enough: «We're a group and one of us has celiac disease: do you have a gluten-free menu and a dedicated kitchen or oven?» Then three questions: is the fryer separate? Are the gluten-free flours stored apart? Does the staff know how to handle celiac disease? At the table, the person with celiac disease tells the waiter just as simply. A printable version is in the restaurant checklist, and the full method in our guide to avoiding cross-contamination at restaurants.

Phrases to avoid

  • «Once won't hurt you»: it does hurt, even when you can't see it.
  • «Are you sure it's really necessary?»: celiac disease is an autoimmune disease, not a fad.
  • «Don't be difficult»: asking how a dish is made is caution, not a whim.
A useful phrase instead: «Tell me what makes you feel at ease and I'll do it».

chapters.title: How to Avoid Cross-Contamination at a Restaurant: The Complete Guide to Eating Gluten-Free Safely
takeaways: Cross-contamination happens when even minimal traces of gluten come into contact with a gluten-free dish through shared utensils, surfaces or frying oil.
AIC-certified venues have passed checks on procedures, suppliers and staff training, but the absence of certification doesn't automatically mean a venue is unsafe.
A dedicated kitchen or oven, a clear menu and trained staff are the most concrete signs of attention to celiac disease, even at uncertified venues.
Always mentioning celiac disease, not a generic intolerance, remains the most effective way to reduce risk at any type of venue.
chapters.html:
What cross-contamination is and why it worries people with celiac disease

If you have celiac disease, you probably already know the feeling: sitting at the table, the menu offers a "gluten-free" dish, but a doubt remains. Knowing how to avoid cross-contamination at a restaurant is the most important question to ask before ordering, because for someone with celiac disease even a minimal amount of gluten, a few crumbs or a utensil used for two different preparations, can trigger an autoimmune reaction, often with no symptoms visible right away. In this guide you'll find the signs of a truly safe venue, the right questions to ask staff, and what to do if something goes wrong. The same basic rules apply at home too: we cover this in our guide on cross-contamination in the kitchen.

How to avoid cross-contamination at a restaurant: the right questions before ordering

Even before looking at the menu, a few questions help you gauge a venue's level of attention to celiac disease right away.

Is the kitchen or oven dedicated?

Always ask, without worrying about seeming intrusive: a work area or oven used exclusively for gluten-free preparations, separate from the one for traditional dishes, is the most concrete guarantee against cross-contamination. If the answer is vague, that's already a first sign to pay attention to.

How are utensils, cutting boards and work surfaces cleaned?

Wooden cutting boards, pasta strainers and grills are porous surfaces that easily retain flour residue even after washing: an attentive venue generally has dedicated utensils, often a different color so they're easy to spot at a glance, never shared with traditional preparations.

Does staff really understand celiac disease?

A trained server can naturally explain how a gluten-free order is handled, from the kitchen to the table. If the request causes hesitation or gets vaguely passed off to the chef with no further detail, cross-contamination is probably not a priority for the venue.

How does the dish arrive at the table?

A gluten-free dish should be visually recognizable too, for example with a colored marker or a clear description when served, and should never pass through the same tray or fryer as dishes containing gluten. For takeaway too, packaging should be sealed separately from other orders.

The signs that a restaurant is truly safe for celiacs

Beyond direct questions, a few objective elements help assess a venue's reliability even before sitting down.

AIC certification: what it really guarantees

Venues certified by the Italian Celiac Association have passed periodic checks on suppliers, kitchen procedures and staff training, checks that repeat over time. It isn't a legal requirement, so its absence doesn't automatically mean a venue is unsafe, but the mark significantly reduces the margin of error compared to a venue that simply calls itself "gluten-free" with no external checks.

A clear gluten-free menu, not a generic one

A good gluten-free menu specifies which dishes are prepared in a dedicated area and which only share the base ingredient with traditional versions: the difference isn't cosmetic, because in the second case the risk of contamination during cooking remains real even if the starting ingredient is gluten-free.

Reviews and reports from other celiacs

The direct experiences of other people with celiac disease often tell you more than any label: venues repeatedly flagged as safe by the community, gathered in verified directories like Mappa Senza Glutine, are a more reliable starting point than a generic Google Maps search.

Pizzerias, à la carte restaurants and bakeries: the risks change by venue type

Not every venue handles cross-contamination the same way: the type of kitchen strongly affects the level of attention required.

Pizzerias: the shared oven is the main risk

Even with a perfectly gluten-free dough, baking pizza in the same wood-fired oven used for traditional dough exposes it to the risk of residual flour on the refractory base: the most attentive pizzerias have a separate baking area or an electric oven dedicated only to gluten-free pizzas.

À la carte restaurants: watch out for shared fryers and work surfaces

In a restaurant with a large menu, the biggest risk involves single fryers used for fries and other breaded fried foods, plus the work surfaces where fresh pasta is rolled out: wheat flour left in the air or on surfaces can settle even on preparations meant to be gluten-free.

Bakeries and pastry shops: flour flies, literally

In bakery and pastry labs, traditional flour easily becomes airborne during processing, which is why bakeries that are truly safe for celiacs often have a physically separate lab, or work on days and hours dedicated exclusively to gluten-free production.

Ice cream shops, fast food and ethnic restaurants: specific risks

A few settings deserve a separate mention: at ice cream shops the main risk is shared scoops and tubs, at fast food chains like McDonald's it's shared fryers, and at ethnic restaurants it's traditional soy sauce, almost always wheat-based.

The essential checklist before sitting down to eat

Before ordering, run through these points mentally: they help you gauge a venue's attention to celiac disease in a few seconds.

  • Ask if the kitchen or oven is dedicated to gluten-free preparations, not just whether they "know how to cook gluten-free".
  • Check for AIC certification, if present, or look for reviews from other celiacs about the venue.
  • Ask staff how the order is handled, from the kitchen through to table service.
  • Watch how the dish arrives: it should be recognizable and shouldn't share trays or utensils with other dishes.
  • Always mention celiac disease, not a generic intolerance, so staff understand the real need for zero contamination.
A printable version is in the restaurant checklist; if you're the one inviting a celiac friend, see our guide on how to behave.

What to do if you suspect contamination after eating out

Even when choosing carefully, you may feel bloating, abdominal pain or fatigue in the hours after a meal out: it doesn't necessarily mean the venue made a mistake, but it's worth reporting. Contacting the venue calmly, explaining the symptoms and the time of your booking, helps staff spot any gaps in their procedure; if the venue is AIC certified, the episode can also be reported to the association, which uses this information for future checks. Isolated symptoms don't necessarily call for an urgent visit, but repeated episodes after eating out are worth discussing with your specialist. A fuller guide to symptoms and timing is what to do after accidental gluten ingestion.

Frequently asked questions about cross-contamination at restaurants

The most common questions from celiacs who want to eat out safely.

How do you avoid cross-contamination at a restaurant?

By choosing venues with a dedicated kitchen or oven, asking staff how gluten-free preparations are handled, and checking that utensils and surfaces aren't shared with traditional dishes. None of these precautions alone eliminates the risk, but together they reduce it significantly, especially at a venue used to handling celiac orders regularly.

Are non-AIC-certified restaurants safe for celiacs?

They can be, but safety depends entirely on direct experience and internal procedures, with no periodic external check to guarantee them. AIC certification isn't a legal requirement, so many safe venues simply haven't applied for it: asking about a dedicated kitchen and staff training remains essential either way.

Is it enough to just order the "gluten-free" dish from the menu to be safe?

No, not always: a dish labeled "gluten-free" can still be contaminated if cooked in the same water, fryer or grill used for gluten-containing food. The label on the menu indicates the absence of gluten among the ingredients, not necessarily the absence of risk during preparation.

How much contamination does it take to feel sick if you have celiac disease?

Minimal amounts, even a few milligrams of gluten, are enough to trigger an immune response in a person with celiac disease, which is why EU regulation sets the "gluten-free" threshold at no more than 20 mg/kg (20 ppm) of product. That's why cross-contamination stays dangerous even when it seems negligible, regardless of symptoms felt right away.

chapters.title: AIC Certification: What It Really Means and How to Spot a Truly Certified Venue
takeaways: AIC (Associazione Italiana Celiachia) is a non-profit association, not a certification body in the technical sense: the programme venues join is called Alimentazione Fuori Casa (AFC).
Joining AFC requires a celiac disease training course for staff, run by the local AIC chapter, the local health authority (ASL) or affiliated bodies, followed by periodic on-site meetings.
The venue's HACCP self-monitoring plan must include gluten as a critical control point, covering raw materials, storage, production, cleaning and service.

"AIC-certified" in everyday language (including on this site) refers to membership in the AFC network: a real level of assurance, verified through periodic checks, even if different from a strict ISO-style certification.
chapters.html:
What "AIC-certified" really means

On social media, in reviews and even on this site, you'll often read "AIC-certified venue" as shorthand for maximum safety for a celiac. It's a useful and widespread expression, but it's worth being precise: AIC (Associazione Italiana Celiachia) is a non-profit association, not a certification body in the way an ISO-accredited organisation would be. The programme venues join is called Alimentazione Fuori Casa (AFC), and it mirrors the methods and safeguards typical of a certification path, even though it isn't one in the strict technical-legal sense. This distinction doesn't diminish the value of the mark: it just means understanding better what's actually behind it before relying on it.

How the AFC programme works

Joining the AFC network isn't a formality: it requires a concrete process for the venue and its staff. If you run a venue and want to join, see our guide Restaurateurs: how to join the AIC program.

Initial training

The first requirement is that staff attend a training course on celiac disease and the gluten-free diet, run by the local AIC chapter, the relevant health authority (ASL) or bodies that partner with the association. Reading the rulebook isn't enough: active participation is required.

Follow-up meetings at the venue

After the initial training, periodic meetings take place directly at the venue, run by the local AIC chapter, to verify that procedures are actually being applied and not just taught once.

HACCP with gluten as a critical control point

The venue's HACCP self-monitoring plan must include gluten as a specific critical control point, covering raw materials used, storage methods, production stages, cleaning procedures and how food is served or sold directly to customers.

What the mark does NOT guarantee, and why that's fine

A venue that joins the AFC programme isn't a sterile environment immune to every possible human error: no system is. What it concretely guarantees is a verified training process, periodic checks over time (not a one-off audit) and written procedures that staff actually know, rather than a generic verbal commitment. That's the practical, verifiable difference between a venue that "says" it can handle gluten-free and one that proves it through a structured process, like La Rosa dei Venti in Milan or Fornerie Alessandrino in Rome, both part of the programme and listed in our directory.

How to actually spot a venue that's part of the programme

Beyond the mark displayed in a window or on a menu, a few concrete signals help distinguish real membership from a generic self-declaration:

  • Staff can explain the procedures without hesitation, rather than vaguely deferring to the chef.
  • A dedicated kitchen or oven, or at least written protocols on how cross-contamination is avoided in shared spaces.
  • The venue appears in AIC's official list or in verified directories like Mappa Senza Glutine, not only in its own promotional material.
  • Updates over time: a venue that's been part of the programme for years has attended multiple follow-up meetings, not just the initial course.
The member restaurants and pizzerias we have checked are on the AIC restaurants map.

Frequently asked questions about AIC certification

The most common questions about what this mark really means.

Is AIC an official certification body?

No, AIC is a non-profit association. The Alimentazione Fuori Casa programme that venues join mirrors the methods of a certification path (training, periodic checks, written procedures), but technically it isn't a certification issued by an independent third-party body in the way ISO certifications are, for example.

Is a venue that hasn't joined the AFC programme necessarily unsafe?

No: many venues handle gluten-free well without having formally joined the programme, whether by organisational choice or because they recently opened. Membership reduces the margin for error thanks to periodic external checks, but its absence doesn't automatically mean higher risk: checking for a dedicated kitchen, staff training and reviews still remains useful.

How can I check whether a venue really is part of the programme?

The most reliable way is to check the official list on the Associazione Italiana Celiachia website, or verified directories like Mappa Senza Glutine, rather than relying only on the mark displayed on a menu or in a window, which can be outdated.

chapters.title: Gluten-Free Pizza in Italy: Where to Eat It and How to Spot a Safe Pizzeria
takeaways: For someone with celiac disease a pizzeria is safe because of how it works, not because of what the menu says: oven, flour and utensils matter.
There are three levels: a 100% gluten-free pizzeria, an AIC member pizzeria and a pizzeria with a simple gluten-free option.
In the directory you'll find 14 AIC member pizzerias in 9 cities, from the most historic to the most recent.
Gluten-free pizza isn't lighter or easier to digest by definition: calories depend on dough and toppings.
chapters.html:
Three levels of safety for gluten-free pizza

Not every «gluten-free pizza» is the same. For someone with celiac disease it helps to tell them apart:

  • 100% gluten-free pizzeria: the whole kitchen is dedicated, so the contamination risk is lowest.
  • AIC member pizzeria: it has followed the training of the Alimentazione Fuori Casa program and follows procedures agreed with the association (what that means is explained in our guide to AIC certification).
  • Pizzeria with a gluten-free option: the dough exists, but the oven and the work surface may not be separate. Here you need precise questions.

What to ask before ordering

A few questions clear up almost everything:

  • Is the oven dedicated, or does the pizza bake on the same stone or tray as the others?
  • Is the dough worked away from wheat flour? Flour in the air and left on the counter can contaminate.
  • Are the peel, the cutter and the boards dedicated?
  • Are the toppings taken from containers that haven't touched hands or utensils used for regular pizzas?
Always say you have celiac disease, not just that you prefer gluten-free. More precautions are in our guide to avoiding cross-contamination at restaurants. The same questions, ready to print, are in the restaurant checklist. According to an AIC document, in mixed pizzerias the contamination risk is very high because flour is airborne and spreads through the venue (more here).

Gluten-free pizzerias by city

These are the AIC member pizzerias we've checked in the directory, city by city. You can also see all of them on the AIC restaurants map.

Gluten-free pizza in Milan

In Milan you'll find Be Bop, a restaurant and pizzeria near the Navigli since 1986, Casa Biga, a high-end pizzeria in the Isola district, and Le Specialità, a historic pizzeria since 1977 with over 50 gluten-free pizzas. All the Milan listings are in the directory; for other suggestions see our guide to gluten-free restaurants in Milan.

Gluten-free pizza in Rome

In Rome: Il Secchio e l'Olivaro in Ostiense, with a wood-fired oven and a dedicated lab since 1999, Fornerie Alessandrino, a pizzeria and grill in the Alessandrino district, and Mangiafuoco Pizza & Grill, with a separate gluten-free kitchen. See also our guide to gluten-free restaurants in Rome.

Gluten-free pizza in Naples

Pizzaioli Veraci is an AIC certified pizzeria with a counter and oven dedicated to gluten-free. More addresses and Neapolitan pastries are in our guide to where to eat gluten-free in Naples.

Gluten-free pizza in Florence and Venice

In Florence there is Ciro & Sons, an AIC certified pizzeria. In Venice, at the Zattere, Pizzeria OKE, with separate kitchens; the city is covered in our guide to gluten-free Venice.

Gluten-free pizza in Palermo, Genoa and Verona

In Palermo Pizzicotto is 100% dedicated to gluten-free. In Genoa there are Franco Pizzeria in Sampierdarena, with a dedicated oven, and I Due Fratelli in Prà. In Verona, opposite the Arena, La Costa in Bra. The cities are in our guides to Palermo, Genoa and Verona.

Gluten-free pizza near Turin

In Venaria Reale, near Turin, La Smorfia has been AIC certified for over 25 years.

Is gluten-free pizza lighter or easier to digest?

For someone with celiac disease, gluten-free pizza is simply the pizza they can eat. For people with no problem with gluten there is no evidence that it is lighter or easier to digest: calories depend on dough and toppings, and gluten-free products are not automatically «light», as we explain in our guide to the gluten-free diet and weight.

Making it at home

If you'd rather make your own, you'll find the recipe with the all-purpose mix and the tricks for a light, crisp dough. The dough needs suitable flours: we cover them in our guide to gluten-free flours.

chapters.title: Gluten-Free Ice Cream: Is It Safe? Lactose, Brands and Ice Cream Cake
takeaways: Milk, cream, sugar and fruit contain no gluten: the risk lies in cones, wafers, biscuits, malt and the way it's served.
Gluten-free and lactose-free are two different things: an ice cream can be one and not the other.
For packaged ice cream it's the individual flavour that counts, not the brand: read the label every time.
A gluten-free ice cream cake is easy at home with gluten-free biscuits and two ice creams whose labels you've checked.
chapters.html:
Is ice cream gluten-free?

Plain ice cream, made with milk, cream, sugar and fruit, is gluten-free in itself. Gluten comes in with what is added or with the serving: cones and wafers (the traditional cone contains gluten), crumbled biscuits, wafer pieces and sprinkles, malt, some ready-made toppings and certain bases or flavourings. In an ice cream shop there is also the risk of contamination between scoops and tubs. How to pick a safe shop is explained in our guide to gluten-free ice cream shops.

Packaged ice cream: how to choose

For branded ice cream there is no list that holds forever, because recipes and flavours change: the individual flavour counts, not the brand. Always read the label: look for the «gluten-free» wording or the Crossed Grain mark and check the ingredient list, where gluten cereals must be highlighted. Flavours with biscuit, wafer, cereals or crunch are the riskiest, and «may contain traces of gluten» is a signal to take seriously. The full method is in our guide to reading food labels.

Gluten-free and lactose-free are not the same thing

They are two independent features. A milk-based ice cream can be gluten-free but contain lactose; a lactose-free ice cream can contain gluten, for example in the cone or the biscuit. To get both you need flavours that guarantee both. Fruit sorbets, normally made with water, sugar and fruit, contain no milk; plant-based ice creams (soy, rice, almond, coconut) are lactose-free, but if they are oat-based you need gluten-free oats: we cover this in our guide to oats. Here too the rule is the same: check the individual product.

Where to eat gluten-free ice cream

In our directory you can filter by ice cream shops and see which ones take part in the AIC program. Among the ones we've checked: Zero Gelato in Milan, Grom in Venice and Gelateria Artigianale Oasi in Verona, all listed as AIC certified. The Grom chain also takes part in the program: you can see it in our guide to gluten-free restaurant chains.

Gluten-free ice cream cake: how to make it

A simple ice cream cake, for a 20 cm tin:

  • 200 g gluten-free biscuits
  • 90 g melted butter
  • 600 g ice cream, in two flavours of 300 g
Crush the biscuits, mix them with the butter and press them onto the bottom of a lined tin; chill for 30 minutes. Soften the first ice cream for about ten minutes, spread it over the base and freeze for an hour. Add the second layer and freeze for at least 4 hours, ideally overnight. Unmould about ten minutes before serving. Check the label of the biscuits and the ice creams, and use clean utensils with no crumbs of bread or biscuits containing gluten.

chapters.title: Gluten-Free McDonald's in Italy: What a Celiac Can Really Eat
takeaways: The Gluten Free Burger, developed with Dr. Schär, is the only item on the McDonald's Italy menu explicitly guaranteed gluten-free.
McDonald's Italy doesn't take part in AIC's Out-of-Home Eating program, so the association doesn't verify its preparation procedures.
Fries, salads and some ice creams don't contain gluten as an ingredient, but McDonald's doesn't guarantee they're free of cross-contamination.
For a meal out with the strongest guarantees, AIC-certified venues or those with a dedicated kitchen remain the safest choice for celiacs.
chapters.html:
Gluten-free McDonald's in Italy: what the company actually says

People searching for information on gluten-free McDonald's in Italy often find conflicting claims online: some say celiacs can eat there without worry, others advise against it entirely.
