The reality, checked against official sources from McDonald's Italy and the Italian Celiac Association (AIC), is more nuanced: only one item on the menu is guaranteed gluten-free, while the rest carries a margin of risk the company itself can't rule out.

The Gluten Free Burger: the only item truly guaranteed

The Gluten Free Burger, developed by McDonald's Italy in collaboration with Dr. Schär, is the only menu item explicitly guaranteed gluten-free: the bun meets the EU threshold for "gluten-free" labeling, no more than 20 mg/kg (20 ppm) of product. In terms of the ingredient's composition, it's therefore a verified option for celiacs. The bun, made by Schär, reaches restaurants in a single sealed pack, and the burger is heated and served still in its packaging, a procedure designed specifically to limit the risk of contamination during preparation.

McDonald's and AIC certification: why there isn't one

Unlike the AIC-certified venues you'll find in our directory, McDonald's Italy doesn't take part in the Italian Celiac Association's Out-of-Home Eating program (AFC). This means AIC doesn't weigh in on the suitability of the food served, the preparation procedures, or staff training at its locations. The company shares information on allergens and product composition on its own, through its website and in restaurants, but without the periodic external check that comes with the AIC mark.

Fries, salads and ice cream: why they aren't guaranteed even though they don't contain gluten as an ingredient

Several menu items don't contain gluten as an ingredient, but that alone isn't enough to make them safe for a celiac in a shared kitchen environment.

French fries

McDonald's fries don't contain gluten as an ingredient, but they're fried in a shared kitchen environment: the company itself doesn't guarantee the absence of cross-contamination, especially during periods when the fryers are also used for other breaded products. The official advice is to always ask staff at the location before ordering.

Salads and ice cream

Green salads without chicken and some ice creams also don't contain gluten as an ingredient, but they share surfaces, utensils or equipment with other menu items: for this reason McDonald's can't guarantee they're fully safe for celiacs, the same way it can't with fries.

The McDonald's menu product by product: what the allergen table says

McDonald's Italy publishes a table on its website (mcdonalds.it/allergeni) listing every menu item with a symbol for each allergen: "x" if the product contains it, "!" if it may contain it through contamination. It's the official tool to check before ordering, because the declared gluten status varies a lot from one product to another even within the same category.

GelaTino soft-serve and milkshakes

The GelaTino soft-serve ice cream and the milkshakes (banana, strawberry, vanilla, chocolate) are dairy-based preparations: the allergen table should still be checked product by product, since the formulation can include flavorings or thickeners that change over time. Don't assume they're gluten-free just because the base flavor suggests it.

McFlurry

McFlurry desserts with toppings like Oreo, Biscoff or chocolate biscuits contain wheat-based biscuits, so gluten for certain: they're among the McDonald's desserts to avoid with the most confidence, not a borderline case like fries or the base ice cream.

So is McDonald's safe for a celiac?

It depends on how much risk you're willing to accept. The Gluten Free Burger, on its own, is a verified option in terms of composition. The rest of the menu, including fries, carries a margin of risk that McDonald's itself doesn't eliminate, due to the lack of a dedicated kitchen and AIC certification. Anyone with celiac disease that's particularly sensitive to cross-contamination, or looking for the most reassurance when eating out, will generally find stronger guarantees at AIC-certified venues or those with a dedicated kitchen, like the ones gathered in the Mappa Senza Glutine directory. If you're looking for a fast food or chain restaurant with a celiac menu developed with AIC, see our guide to gluten-free Old Wild West and the one on gluten-free restaurant chains.

Frequently asked questions about McDonald's and the gluten-free diet

The most searched questions about McDonald's and celiac disease in Italy.

Is McDonald's Gluten Free Burger really gluten-free?

Yes, the bun meets the legal threshold for "gluten-free" labeling (no more than 20 mg/kg), thanks to the collaboration between McDonald's Italy and Dr. Schär in developing the product. That said, it only covers the bun's composition, not the whole preparation environment at the location.

Is McDonald's AIC certified?

No, McDonald's Italy doesn't take part in the Italian Celiac Association's Out-of-Home Eating program, so the association doesn't weigh in on the safety of its preparations or staff training at its restaurants.

Are McDonald's fries safe for celiacs?

They aren't guaranteed: while they don't contain gluten as an ingredient, McDonald's itself doesn't rule out cross-contamination during frying in a shared kitchen, especially when the fryers are also used for other breaded products.

Is McDonald's ice cream gluten-free?

The GelaTino soft-serve and the milkshakes are dairy-based, but the formulation should always be checked on the official allergen table product by product: McDonald's still doesn't guarantee an absence of cross-contamination in the preparation environment.

Does McFlurry contain gluten?

McFlurry desserts with biscuit-based toppings, like Oreo or Biscoff, contain gluten for certain because of the biscuit itself: they're among the products to avoid, not a borderline case.

Where can I find the allergen list for McDonald's products?

On the official McDonald's Italy website, at mcdonalds.it/allergeni, and at individual locations, updated periodically by the company based on supplier data.

parts.intro: How much the gluten-free diet costs, which rules protect it and where to shop.

chapters.title: How Much Does a Gluten-Free Diet Cost? Costs, Vouchers and Tax Deductions
takeaways: According to a survey by the consumer research centre C.R.C. with Assoutenti, gluten-free products cost from about a third more to over three times more than their gluten-containing equivalents: +110% for pasta, +257% for rusks.
Italy's National Health Service provides a monthly voucher usable at pharmacies and partner stores to buy certified substitute products.
The voucher amount varies by age and gender and is periodically updated by the Ministry of Health.
Some healthcare expenses related to celiac disease are also tax-deductible on your annual tax return.
chapters.html:
Why a gluten-free diet costs more

Anyone diagnosed with celiac disease soon runs into a practical reality: gluten-free products, especially bread, pasta and baked goods, are on average priced higher than their traditional equivalents, due to dedicated production chains, stricter controls and lower production volumes. Knowing the economic support tools provided by Italy's National Health Service helps manage this expense without giving up quality or food safety. For the latest on vouchers and regulations, see our 2026 regulatory updates for celiacs.

The monthly voucher for gluten-free products

Here's how Italy's main economic support tool for celiacs actually works. The full legal picture is on our celiac disease rules page.

How to get the monthly voucher

After a celiac disease diagnosis, the specialist doctor issues a certification that lets you apply at your local ASL (health authority) for a monthly voucher funded by the National Health Service, usable, depending on the region, at pharmacies, specialty shops and partner supermarkets to buy gluten-free products listed in the Ministry of Health's national register of gluten-free foods. Although it's often called the "AIC voucher", it isn't issued by AIC, which is a patients' association: it's issued by the health service through the ASL.

How much the voucher is worth and how it works

The amount varies by age and gender brackets, set and updated by the Ministry of Health, and is generally higher for teenagers still growing. The voucher is loaded onto the health card or, where the digital system isn't active yet, issued on paper, depending on the region of residence, and can only be used for products listed in the national register.

Tax deductions related to celiac disease

Besides the monthly voucher, some healthcare expenses closely tied to managing celiac disease, such as specialist visits or diagnostic tests not covered by the National Health Service, may qualify as deductible expenses on your tax return: it's always advisable to keep receipts and check with an accountant or tax assistance center which items are actually deductible for the relevant tax year.

How to save money without compromising on safety

A few precautions help keep costs down without ever compromising on food safety:

  • Always use the monthly voucher for staples like bread, pasta and flours, where the savings are greatest.
  • Focus on naturally gluten-free foods like rice, corn, legumes and vegetables, often cheaper than packaged substitute products.
  • Compare prices between pharmacies, supermarkets and specialty stores, which can vary significantly for the same product: our gluten-free shopping at discount stores guide compares Aldi, Lidl and Eurospin, and our guide on where to buy gluten-free products explains the pros and cons of each channel.
  • Cook at home when possible, such as fresh pasta, to cut the cost of ready-made products.

chapters.title: 2026 Regulatory Updates: What Changes for Celiacs in Italy
takeaways: Italy's 2026 Budget Law (art. 77) digitalizes the gluten-free product voucher, making it usable anywhere in the country.
Until now the voucher could only be used in your region of residence: digitalization removes that limit.
The maximum monthly amount stays the same: what changes is the format (digital) and where it can be spent, not its value.
€2 million are allocated for 2026 and €1 million a year from 2027 to implement the system, with regions still to finalize agreements with participating stores.
chapters.html:
The main change: the voucher goes digital and national

Article 77 of Italy's 2026 Budget Law officially introduces the digitalization of the National Health Service's gluten-free product voucher: no more paper vouchers tied to your local health authority (ASL), but a digital system loaded onto your health card or a personal electronic code. The most concrete change for anyone who lives or travels outside their home region is that the voucher becomes usable anywhere in Italy, removing the limit that previously restricted it to your region of residence: participating pharmacies, para-pharmacies, specialty stores and large retailers will be able to accept it wherever you are.

What does NOT change

The maximum monthly amount stays the same: the reform changes the format (from paper to digital) and where it can be spent, not the voucher's economic value, which still varies by age and gender bracket as explained in our guide on how much the gluten-free diet costs.

Implementation timeline

€2 million are allocated for 2026 and €1 million a year from 2027 to put the digitalization into practice. Regions will need to sign agreements with participating stores, and a decree from the Ministry of Health, together with the Ministry of Economy, will define the operational details: actual rollout timing may therefore vary by region.

New guidelines for the restaurant industry

Several Italian regions are updating HACCP guidelines for restaurants, with stricter requirements for venues seeking celiac certification.

What to do in the meantime, while waiting for rollout

Until your region activates the new digital system, the traditional paper voucher remains valid under the current rules, so it's still usable only in your region of residence. It's worth keeping an eye on communications from your local ASL and from the Italian Celiac Association, which is closely following the reform's implementation and publishes updates as regions finalize their agreements with participating stores. All the rules on one updated page: celiac disease rules in Italy.

chapters.title: Where to Buy Gluten-Free Products: Supermarkets, Pharmacies and Specialty Shops
takeaways: Gluten-free products are sold through four main channels: supermarkets, pharmacies, specialty shops and online.
The National Health Service's monthly voucher can be spent, depending on the region, at pharmacies, drugstores, specialty shops and partner supermarkets.
The voucher only covers products listed in the Ministry of Health's national register of gluten-free foods.
Under Italy's 2026 Budget Law, the voucher becomes digital and usable throughout Italy as regions roll out the new system.
chapters.html:
The four channels for gluten-free shopping

People on a gluten-free diet have far more options today than in the past. Each channel has different strengths and limits, though, especially for those using the monthly celiac voucher: it's worth knowing them to decide where to buy what.

Supermarkets

Almost every chain has a section or corner dedicated to gluten-free products, often with own-brand ranges, including at discount stores: Eurospin with "Amo Essere Senza Glutine" and Aldi with "Enjoy Free", which we cover in our guide to gluten-free shopping at discount stores. The supermarket is the most convenient place for naturally gluten-free foods such as rice, legumes, vegetables and meat, and for many packaged products. The downside: the range of substitute products, especially fresh ones, is often smaller, and the voucher can only be used at stores that have an agreement with your region.

Pharmacies

Pharmacies are the traditional channel for gluten-free products and the one where the voucher is most widely accepted. Some dedicate a whole section to food for people with celiac disease, such as Farmacia Santa Rita in Garbatella, Rome. The most common drawback is price, often higher than in large retail for the same product. You'll find the pharmacies in our directory in the pharmacies section.

Specialty shops

Shops dedicated to gluten-free food offer the widest range, often with fresh products from their own kitchen, and many accept the voucher. A few examples from our directory:

  • Milano Senza Glutine, a dedicated shop with a kitchen for bread and fresh pasta, part of a chain with several stores in Lombardy;
  • Gusto Libero in Verona, with over 100 gluten-free and lactose-free products, with an agreement with the local health authority (ULSS) for vouchers;
  • Celiachiamo in Rome, a gluten-free bakery and pastry shop that accepts ASL prescriptions;
  • La Gouterie in Bari, with packaged products that can be bought with the ASL voucher.
The full list is in the specialty shops section.

Online

Manufacturers' websites and specialist online stores offer the widest choice and home delivery, useful for anyone living far from a dedicated shop. Before buying online with the voucher, though, check with your ASL whether it's possible: it depends on the agreements your region has in place.

Where the celiac voucher can be spent

The monthly voucher is funded by the National Health Service and is requested from your local ASL after diagnosis. Where it can be spent depends on the region: in Emilia-Romagna, Sicily, Piedmont and Abruzzo, for example, it can be used at pharmacies, specialty shops and partner supermarkets, and in several regions at drugstores too.

Which products can be bought

Only those listed in the Ministry of Health's national register of gluten-free foods, in the categories provided for: bread and savory baked goods, pasta and pizza, mixes for cakes, bread and pizza, sweet baked goods and breakfast cereals. AIC's Prontuario is something else: it's a voluntary list of products suitable for people with celiac disease, not the list of products that can be bought with the voucher.

What changes in 2026

Article 77 of Italy's 2026 Budget Law makes the voucher digital and usable throughout Italy, no longer only in your region of residence, as regions roll out the new system. The details are in our article on 2026 regulatory updates, while amounts and deductions are in our guide on how much a gluten-free diet costs.

How to organize your shopping

  • Use the voucher for substitute products such as bread, pasta, flours and baked goods, which are the most expensive.
  • Buy naturally gluten-free foods at the supermarket, such as rice, corn, legumes, vegetables, meat and fish.
  • Compare prices for the same product across pharmacies, supermarkets and specialty shops.
  • Always check for the "gluten-free" claim on the label, whatever the channel: see our guide on how to read food labels.
To find a store or a venue in your area see our guide to finding gluten-free places near you.

If you shop on your own in Italy, even as a tourist

Three moves are enough. Recognise the products: look for the «gluten-free» wording or the Crossed Grain mark, and read the ingredient list (reading food labels). Choose the channel: discount stores have dedicated lines, like Eurospin's «Amo Essere Senza Glutine», Aldi's «Enjoy Free» and Lidl's gluten-free Realforno items, while pharmacies and specialty shops usually have the widest range (details in gluten-free shopping at discount stores). Check every time: the range changes from store to store. The monthly voucher is a measure for celiacs covered by the Italian National Health Service: if you aren't, only price and label matter. The rules in detail are on our celiac disease rules page.

parts.title: Travel, family and the unexpected
parts.intro: When you step out of your routine: holidays, children at school, weaning and what to do if gluten arrives by mistake.

chapters.title: Traveling Gluten-Free: 7 Tips for a Safe Holiday
takeaways: Look up certified restaurants and hotels at your destination before you leave and save them to a shared map.
The multilingual AIC card helps you explain celiac disease to restaurant staff abroad.
Request gluten-free airline meals at least 48 hours ahead, and always pack safe snacks as backup.
Local directories and online communities are the most reliable resource off the beaten tourist path.
chapters.html:
Before you leave

Looking up certified restaurants and hotels at your destination ahead of time, saving addresses to a shared map, reduces stress during the trip. For a hotel or resort stay, our guide on AIC-certified hotels and resorts explains what the certification actually guarantees, while our roundup of the best Italian cities for a gluten-free vacation helps you choose a destination.

The celiac translation card

AIC provides a card explaining celiac disease translated into several languages, extremely useful for communicating with restaurant staff abroad.

On planes and trains

Many airlines offer gluten-free meals on request, to be booked at least 48 hours in advance. It's still wise to always carry safe snacks just in case. The details on the special GFML meal and what to bring on board are in our guide on flying gluten-free.

Finding safe places on the spot

Local directories and online communities dedicated to celiacs are the most reliable resource for discovering verified businesses even off the main tourist routes. If you're traveling to Italy, see our gluten-free travel guide for visitors to Italy.

Learn the key words in the local language

Beyond the AIC card, knowing how to say "gluten-free" and "contamination" in the local language helps you get your point across in informal situations too, like a café or a market, where the card alone might not fully clarify your request.

Choose lodging with a kitchenette, if you can

An apartment or room with a small kitchenette lets you prepare part of your meals yourself, reducing reliance on restaurants during the busiest days of the trip: especially useful in less touristy destinations, where finding verified venues can take more time.

Always pack an extra stash of safe snacks

Beyond snacks for the flight, it's worth having a small stash for the whole trip: delays, connections or unpredictable days can leave you without a safe meal nearby, especially in the first hours in a new city.

chapters.title: AIC-Certified Hotels and Resorts for Celiacs: How to Choose a Worry-Free Vacation
takeaways: An AIC-certified hotel guarantees safe gluten-free breakfast and staff trained on celiac disease, not just generic "gluten-free-friendly" claims.
At full-board resorts, certification covers the entire kitchen and meal management, not just breakfast.
Even without certification, some properties offer in-room kitchenettes or arrangements with nearby certified restaurants.
Booking ahead and mentioning celiac disease when you book, not on arrival, remains the golden rule for a surprise-free vacation.
chapters.html:
AIC-certified hotels: why they make a difference on vacation

On vacation, managing celiac disease changes compared to your routine at home: you don't have your own kitchen, you eat out more often, and often at properties you don't know. Choosing AIC-certified hotels and resorts for celiacs means relying on properties that have passed specific checks on breakfast, kitchen management and staff training, instead of finding out on arrival whether the property is actually equipped. In this guide we look at what the certification really guarantees and how to plan a worry-free vacation.

What an AIC-certified hotel actually guarantees

The certification isn't a generic label: it covers specific, verifiable aspects of the property. If you want to understand in detail how the AIC programme behind this mark works, for restaurants and other venues too, see our guide on what "AIC certification" really means.

Safe gluten-free breakfast

Gluten-free bread, cookies, cereal and pastries prepared or stored separately from other products, to avoid the cross-contamination typical of shared buffets.

Staff trained on celiac disease

Dining room and kitchen staff receive specific training on how to handle gluten-free requests and preparations, reducing the risk of mistakes from carelessness or limited knowledge of the topic.

Kitchen equipped for full meals

At properties with an in-house restaurant, certification can also cover lunch and dinner, with dishes prepared avoiding contact with gluten-containing ingredients.

Full-board resorts: what changes compared to a classic hotel

At full-board resorts, managing celiac disease is more complex, since it covers every meal of the day, often in buffet format.

The risk of shared buffets

Self-service buffets, typical of resorts, raise the risk of contamination: utensils shared between different trays, crumbs moving from one dish to another. An AIC-certified resort has dedicated stations or staff who serve gluten-free dishes directly.

Themed dinners and show cooking

Themed evenings and show cooking, common at resorts, need extra attention: always check with staff whether gluten-free alternatives are planned for that specific evening, ideally mentioning it at check-in.

How to find AIC-certified hotels and resorts for your vacation

The most reliable way is to check the certification directly on the property's website or ask for confirmation before booking, rather than trusting generic self-declared labels like "gluten-free friendly" found on booking platforms. The list of properties in AIC's Alimentazione Fuori Casa program is published in the printed guide, on AIC's website (where it's updated in real time) and in the free app for members, with a map of participating venues. In the Mappa Senza Glutine directory you'll find verified properties, with a clear indication of whether the certification is confirmed or not.

Not just hotels: B&Bs, farm stays and holiday homes

AIC's program isn't limited to hotels: participating properties include rented rooms, farm stays, B&Bs, holiday homes and holiday villages. Venues in the network are periodically monitored by professionals who support the staff and check that requirements are still met. An example in our directory is Hotel Al Piave in Venice, in the Castello district near St Mark's Square: it's listed as one of the few hotels in the city with AIC certification and offers an entirely gluten-free breakfast. Planning a city break? See also our guides to gluten-free Venice and the best Italian cities for a gluten-free vacation.

What to do if the hotel isn't AIC certified

Even without certification, a gluten-free vacation is possible with a bit more care: check if the room has a kitchenette or a small fridge to store safe snacks and products brought from home, look for AIC-certified restaurants or ones flagged by the community nearby for lunch and dinner, and always bring a stock of gluten-free products for emergencies, especially in less touristy destinations where finding them locally can be difficult.

Frequently asked questions about gluten-free hotels and resorts

The most common questions from celiacs planning a vacation.

What does it mean that a hotel is AIC certified?

It means the property has passed specific checks from the Italian Celiac Association on breakfast, any in-house dining and staff training, with periodic reviews over time.

Are full-board resorts safe for celiacs?

They can be if AIC certified or with dedicated buffet procedures: without these guarantees, the risk of cross-contamination in self-service formats is higher than at an à la carte restaurant.

Do I need to tell the hotel about celiac disease before arriving?

Yes, it's strongly recommended to mention it when booking, not at check-in: the kitchen needs time to organize breakfast and meals safely, especially during peak season.

What should I bring on vacation if the hotel isn't certified?

A stock of basic gluten-free products (bread, snacks, pasta) for emergencies, especially if the destination is less touristy: they can be hard to find locally outside major cities.

chapters.title: Celiac Kids at School: Managing Cafeterias and Field Trips
takeaways: A gluten-free school meal is a legal right in Italy, at no extra cost for the family.
A medical certificate submitted to the school office is enough to agree on the menu with catering.
Informing teachers ahead of time and packing safe snacks prevents issues during field trips.
Involving your child in choosing gluten-free treats to share helps them enjoy socializing without feeling different.
chapters.html:
The school cafeteria: what the law says

In Italy, the right to a gluten-free meal in school cafeterias is guaranteed by law no. 123 of 4 July 2005, which requires school and hospital cafeterias, and other public facilities, to provide gluten-free meals on request: a piece of legislation that's practically unique in the world. In practice, it's enough to submit the medical certificate to the school office and agree on the menu with the catering service, at no extra cost to the family: the law also provides national funds distributed to the regions, used both to buy gluten-free ingredients and to train kitchen staff. According to the Ministry of Health's latest report to Parliament, in 2024 33,027 public cafeterias served gluten-free meals, 22,972 of them in schools. For families approaching weaning, our guide on gluten and weaning explains when and how to introduce it according to the latest research.

Inclusion at the table: why separate tables aren't needed

The Italian Celiac Association's guidelines are clear on one point: a gluten-free meal shouldn't be treated as an exception to be set apart. A celiac child is entitled to a balanced meal of equivalent quality to their classmates', eaten at the same table, not at a separate one: it's as much a matter of food safety as of the child's experience at school.

Field trips and school outings

Informing teachers ahead of time and, if needed, providing safe snacks to bring along prevents uncomfortable situations during outings away from school. For everyday snack ideas, see our guide on gluten-free school snacks.

Birthday parties and socializing

Involving the child in choosing gluten-free sweets and snacks to share with classmates helps them enjoy social life without feeling different.

chapters.title: Weaning and Gluten: When to Introduce It and What Research Says
takeaways: According to ESPGHAN guidelines, gluten can be introduced at any point between 4 and 12 months of age.
Studies have debunked the idea that introducing gluten earlier or later reduces the risk of developing celiac disease.
Neither the duration of breastfeeding nor whether it continues through weaning affects the onset of the condition.
The only established risk factor remains genetic, tied to the HLA region of DNA, which is why screening first-degree relatives is recommended.
chapters.html:
A recommendation that changed over time

For years parents were told there was an "ideal window" for introducing gluten, and that respecting it could protect a child from celiac disease. It's one of the recommendations research has revised most thoroughly: we now know that the moment gluten enters the diet doesn't change the probability of developing the condition. Understanding what the guidelines actually say makes weaning less anxious, especially when there's already a celiac in the family.

What the guidelines say today

The European reference is the European Society for Paediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology and Nutrition (ESPGHAN).

The 4-12 month window

According to ESPGHAN, gluten can be introduced at any point between 4 and 12 months of age, with no specific timing within that window proving preferable to others in terms of prevention.

Why chasing a date doesn't help

Studies on genetically at-risk children showed that neither early nor late introduction changes the probability of developing celiac disease in childhood. Late introduction seems at most to delay the appearance of symptoms, not prevent the condition.

What about breastfeeding?

Here too the literature corrected a widespread belief: the duration of breastfeeding and whether it continues through weaning don't affect the onset of celiac disease. This takes nothing away from the value of breastfeeding for all the other reasons it's recommended: it simply shouldn't be treated as a tool for preventing celiac disease, because it isn't one.

What actually matters: genetics

The only established risk factor identified so far is genetic, tied to a specific region of DNA known as HLA. It's why celiac disease runs in families and why screening first-degree relatives is recommended even without symptoms. If there are confirmed cases in the family, discussing it with your pediatrician before weaning is more useful than chasing the "right" month for a first biscuit. When a diagnosis does arrive, our guide to school meals and trips covers the next stage.

Frequently asked questions about weaning and gluten

The most common doubts from parents, especially where celiac disease runs in the family.

Should I delay gluten if there's a celiac in the family?

Current evidence doesn't support delay as a protective strategy: gluten can be introduced in the 4-12 month window as for any other child. What does make sense, with a family history, is discussing it with your pediatrician and knowing which symptoms to watch for.

If my child develops celiac disease, is it because of how I weaned them?

No. The only established risk factor is genetic: neither the timing of gluten introduction nor breastfeeding practices determine the onset of the condition.

How much gluten should I give at the start?

There's no demonstrated "protective" amount: introduction follows normal weaning practice, gradually and alongside other foods, according to the guidance of the pediatrician following the child.

chapters.title: Accidental Gluten Ingestion: What to Do If Someone With Celiac Disease Eats It by Mistake
takeaways: There is no specific treatment that blocks gluten already swallowed: AIC advises not to panic.
Symptoms, when they appear, show up from one or two hours to 24-48 hours later; some people have none at all.
Drinking water, resting and going straight back to a gluten-free diet are the points the sources agree on.
If symptoms don't go away or episodes repeat, see a doctor. This guide is informational and doesn't replace medical advice.
chapters.html:
The short answer

If someone with celiac disease swallows gluten by mistake, there is no specific treatment that blocks it. AIC advises not to panic and to wait for the symptoms to pass: according to AIC they usually resolve within a few hours. If the problems don't go away on their own, it's the doctor who assesses treatment for the symptoms. This guide is informational and doesn't replace medical advice.

Which symptoms can appear and when

The most described symptoms are abdominal pain, headache, diarrhea, nausea or vomiting, a general feeling of being unwell and tiredness. They can appear from one or two hours after ingestion up to 24 hours, and in many cases even 24-48 hours later. How long they last varies: the sources don't agree, and range from a few hours to several days. Not everyone has symptoms: some people feel nothing, but damage to the intestine can still occur, which is why no symptoms is not a green light.

What you can do in the following hours

The sources agree on a few simple things:

  • Drink water, especially with vomiting or diarrhea.
  • Rest and eat lightly until you feel better.
  • Go straight back to a gluten-free diet, with no more exceptions.
We give no advice on medication: symptoms are treated only on a doctor's advice.

When to call the doctor

It's worth contacting the doctor or gastroenterologist who follows you if symptoms don't go away, if they're very strong or if episodes repeat. It's also worth telling them about accidental exposures, especially if you notice they happen often: they may point to something in your routine that needs fixing. To understand the condition better there is our guide to what celiac disease is.

How to stop it happening

Almost always the mistake comes from contamination or a label misread. At home what counts is cross-contamination in the kitchen, away from home how to avoid it at a restaurant, and for packaged products how to read labels and our guide to doubtful ingredients. Venues that take part in the AIC program follow procedures agreed with the association: you'll find them on the AIC restaurants map.
